content: 1. Iron-fortified rice does not significantly increase hemoglobin levels in preschool-aged children, as demonstrated in a study published in the Journal of Rice Research in 2013. 2. A blinded, cluster-randomized, placebo-controlled school feeding trial conducted in Burundi evaluated the effects of rice fortified with iron, zinc, thiamine, and folic acid. The results, published in the Food and Nutrition Bulletin in 2015, highlighted the potential benefits of such interventions in school-aged populations. 3. A double-blind, cluster-randomized controlled trial in Cambodia assessed the impact of multi-micronutrient-fortified rice on hemoglobin, iron, and vitamin A status in schoolchildren. The findings, published in Nutrients in 2016, demonstrated improvements in these nutritional markers. 4. In Thailand, extruded rice grains fortified with zinc, iron, and vitamin A were incorporated into a school lunch program. This intervention increased zinc status among Thai schoolchildren, as reported in the Journal of Nutrition in 2013. 5. Triple-fortified rice containing vitamin A was shown to reduce marginal vitamin A deficiency and increase liver vitamin A stores in school-aged Thai children. These findings were published in the Journal of Nutrition in 2014. 6. A study conducted in India demonstrated that micronized ferric pyrophosphate delivered through extruded rice kernels improved body iron stores in children. This double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled midday meal feeding trial was published in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition in 2011. 7. Field trials in the Philippines explored the artificial enrichment of white rice as a solution to endemic beriberi. The results, published in the Journal of Nutrition in 1950, provided evidence supporting this approach. 8. A study in India investigated the effects of multiple micronutrient-fortified rice on physical performance, plasma vitamin B12 levels, and homocysteine concentrations in schoolchildren. The findings, published in the Journal of Nutrition in 2012, highlighted the potential benefits of such fortification. 9. The stability of vitamin A, iron, and zinc in fortified rice during storage was evaluated in Cambodia. The study, published in Nutrients in 2016, emphasized the importance of maintaining nutrient stability for future national standards and programs. 10. Research on the stability of vitamin A in triple-fortified extruded rice grains containing iron, zinc, and vitamin A was published in the International Journal of Food Science and Technology in 2012. The study demonstrated the feasibility of maintaining vitamin A stability in fortified rice. 11. The stability of folic acid in fortified extruded Ultra Rice® was assessed under prolonged storage conditions at 40°C and 60% relative humidity. The findings, published in the International Journal of Food Science and Technology in 2011, highlighted the challenges of maintaining folic acid stability in fortified rice formulations. 12. Cooking methods were shown to affect the stability of thiamine and folic acid in fortified rice. This study, published in the International Journal of Food Science and Nutrition in 2017, emphasized the importance of cooking practices in preserving nutrient content. 13. Artisanal parboiling methods in Ghana were found to alter the thiamine and riboflavin content of rice. The study, published in Tropical Science in 2007, highlighted the impact of traditional processing techniques on nutrient retention. 14. A review of the global prevalence of folate and vitamin B12 deficiencies was published in the Food and Nutrition Bulletin in 2008. The study underscored the widespread nature of these deficiencies and the need for targeted interventions. 15. The case for vitamin B12 fortification of flour was discussed in a review published in the Food and Nutrition Bulletin in 2010. The authors highlighted the potential public health benefits of such fortification strategies. 16. A report by the Pan American Health Organization, March of Dimes, and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommended levels of folic acid and vitamin B12 fortification. These conclusions were published in Nutrition Reviews in 2004. 17. Co-fortification of ferric pyrophosphate and citric acid/trisodium citrate into extruded rice grains was shown to double iron bioavailability. This study, published in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition in 2016, demonstrated the effectiveness of in situ generation of soluble ferric pyrophosphate citrate complexes. 18. The World Health Organization (WHO) has developed guidelines for the fortification of rice with vitamins and minerals as a public health strategy. These guidelines emphasize the importance of evidence-based approaches to address micronutrient deficiencies. 19. The GRADE Working Group has established a framework for rating the quality of evidence and the strength of recommendations. This framework is widely used in public health and clinical research to ensure transparency and reliability in decision-making. 20. The effectiveness of food fortification programs in reducing anemia prevalence and improving hemoglobin concentrations was evaluated in Costa Rica. The findings, published in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition in 2015, demonstrated the success of these interventions in women and children. 21. The WHO has published guidelines on daily iron supplementation for infants, children, adult women, and adolescent girls. These guidelines aim to address iron deficiency and anemia in vulnerable populations. 22. The Codex Alimentarius provides general principles for the addition of essential nutrients to foods. These principles guide the development of national and international standards for food fortification. 23. The stability of fortified nutrients during storage and processing is critical for the success of fortification programs. Research in this area informs the development of effective strategies to maintain nutrient content in fortified foods. 24. The WHO's e-Library of Evidence for Nutrition Actions (eLENA) provides a comprehensive resource for evidence-based nutrition interventions. This platform supports the implementation of effective public health strategies worldwide. 25. The WHO's Global Nutrition Targets 2025 aim to reduce anemia prevalence and improve nutritional status globally. These targets are supported by evidence-based policy briefs and guidelines. 26. The WHO's handbook for guideline development provides a systematic approach to creating evidence-based recommendations. This resource ensures the rigor and transparency of the guideline development process. 27. The Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions offers guidance on conducting high-quality systematic reviews. This resource is essential for synthesizing evidence in public health and clinical research. 28. The WHO's Vitamin and Mineral Nutrition Information System (VMNIS) tracks global progress in addressing micronutrient deficiencies. This system provides valuable data for monitoring and evaluating nutrition programs. 29. The WHO's guidelines for the declaration of interests ensure transparency and accountability in the development of public health recommendations. These guidelines are critical for maintaining the integrity of expert advisory panels and committees.
